screens.title: SQL Fundamentals: SELECT, FROM, WHERE
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will learn how to speak to relational databases using S Q L. S Q L is a declarative language, which means you tell the database what you want rather than how to get it. You'll learn three fundamentals: how to name the columns you need with SELECT, how to tell the database which table to read from with FROM, and how to narrow the rows returned with WHERE. These three clauses form the backbone of most queries you will write. We'll see concrete examples using a Students table and a Products table, compare selecting every column versus specific columns, and practice common filters using numeric and string comparisons. Along the way I'll point out small mistakes that commonly change results, like forgetting to repeat the column name when using OR, or mixing strings and numbers. By the end you'll be able to write clear read-only queries that retrieve precisely the data needed for reports, UIs, or analysis. Think of S Q L as asking a very literal librarian for the exact pages you need—being precise saves time and avoids errors.

screens.title: What is SQL and why declarative matters
screens.narratorSegment: S Q L stands for Structured Query Language and it is the standard way to communicate with relational databases. Unlike an imperative language where you specify step-by-step how to compute a result, S Q L is declarative: you describe the result you want and the database figures out the best way to deliver it. That distinction matters because it changes how you think about problems. For example, when you ask for student first and last names, you don't tell the database how to scan files or which index to use. You simply say you want those columns from the Students table and optionally which rows to keep. A common misconception is to treat S Q L like a general-purpose programming language and try to write procedural loops inside queries; instead, keep logic expressed as set-based operations and filters. Concrete example: to list every student's name you declare the columns and the table; you do not loop through rows in application code and build results manually. Takeaway: thinking declaratively leads to simpler queries and lets the database optimize execution. Question to carry forward: what difference does declarative style make when tables contain millions of rows?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › What is SQL?
Definition

SQL is declarative

You say what you want, not how to get it. This frees the database to optimize retrieval for you.

Concrete example
Request first and last names from Students and let the DB decide scanning or indexing.
Common misconception
Treating SQL like a step-by-step script and attempting procedural loops inside queries leads to complexity and poor performance.
Key takeaway
Write set-based, declarative queries and rely on the DB optimizer for execution details.
Analogy
Think of SQL as telling a librarian which books and pages you need rather than instructing them to walk through each shelf one by one.
Try this mentally
SELECT FirstName, LastName
FROM Students;
This small query declares the desired columns and table; the database chooses how to fetch them efficiently.

screens.title: SELECT basics
screens.narratorSegment: The SELECT clause specifies the columns you want to retrieve from a table. At its simplest you can list column names separated by commas, which returns only those fields for every row. Listing columns is useful when you want to limit network transfer or simplify results for a report. A common beginner step is to use SELECT with the Students table to get first and last names. Concrete example: a query that selects FirstName and LastName from Students returns only those two columns for every student. A frequent misconception is to assume columns will be returned in alphabetical order—S Q L returns columns in the order you list them. Also remember that selecting fewer columns is not only cleaner but faster when tables are wide. The code panel shows a small walkthrough starting with selecting all columns for inspection and then narrowing to specific columns. Takeaway: prefer explicit column lists in production, and use the all-columns form only for quick exploration. How might you choose columns differently for a public report versus an internal debug session? SELECT basics means list only the columns you need. this reduces data size and improves clarity and performance.. In practical terms, how to choose which columns to retrieve. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: SELECT * versus specific columns
screens.narratorSegment: Using the asterisk in SELECT returns every column from the specified table. This is useful for quick exploration, debugging, or when you genuinely need all fields. However, there are important tradeoffs: returning unnecessary columns increases data transfer and can unintentionally expose sensitive fields during development. Conversely, selecting specific columns is explicit, easier to read, and often faster because the database can avoid reading wide fields. Concrete example: selecting all columns from Students might return SocialSecurity or other private attributes you didn't intend to show. A common beginner mistake is leaving SELECT * in code that runs in production, thereby sending extra data to an A P I or UI. Another subtle point is that selecting specific columns preserves column order as you expect; S Q L will present columns in the sequence you list. Takeaway: use the asterisk sparingly and prefer explicit lists for stable, secure queries. Ask yourself: which columns are truly required for this view or report? screens.title: FROM clause: naming the source table
screens.narratorSegment: The FROM clause identifies the table that contains the columns you requested. It is essential because column names mean nothing without the context of a table. If two tables share a column name, the FROM clause plus table-qualified column names resolve ambiguity. A simple example: when you write FROM Students, the database knows to look for columns such as FirstName or GPA on that table. A common misunderstanding is thinking FROM can be omitted when running quick tests; omitting the table will produce a syntax error. Another point: even for simple SELECT queries the order is SELECT then FROM then WHERE — this order expresses intent clearly and is how S Q L parsers expect queries to be formed. Takeaway: always know which table holds your data and, when necessary, qualify column names with the table to avoid collisions. Reflect: if multiple tables contain a column named ID, how will you ensure the query returns the intended field? FROM clause: naming the source table means from specifies the table to read rows from; it gives column names context and prevents ambiguity.. In practical terms, tell the database where to read rows from. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › FROM clause

Purpose

Name the table that contains the columns you select so the database knows where to look for data.

SELECT FirstName, LastName
FROM Students;
Ambiguity note
If two tables have the same column name, qualify it using TableName.ColumnName to be explicit.
Concrete scenario
An application joining Courses and Students might have an ID column in each table; always qualify to avoid returning the wrong ID.
Key Takeaway

FROM tells the database which table to scan — it anchors column names and prevents ambiguity in queries.

screens.title: WHERE clause fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: The WHERE clause filters which rows are returned by the query. It appears after FROM and contains one or more conditions built from comparison operators. Use WHERE to express criteria like "GPA greater than 3.5" or "Major equals Computer Science." Comparisons compare a column to a value or another column; string values must be enclosed in single quotes, while numeric values are unquoted. A typical process is: first write SELECT and FROM to choose columns and table, then add a WHERE clause to narrow rows. Concrete example: to find students majoring in Computer Science, you add a condition where Major equals that string. A common error is to omit quotes around strings or to write OR clauses without repeating the column name, which can make the condition always true. Takeaway: use WHERE to reduce the result set to only relevant rows and double-check string quoting to ensure correct matches. Try to phrase your filter as a simple condition first, then add combinations if needed. WHERE clause fundamentals means where filters rows using comparisons; string literals require single quotes and numeric literals should remain unquoted.. In practical terms, filter rows using comparisons. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Step-by-step
-- Find Computer Science majors
SELECT FirstName, LastName, Major
FROM Students
WHERE Major = 'Computer Science';

-- Numeric filter example
SELECT FirstName, LastName, GPA
FROM Students
WHERE GPA >= 3.5;
Notes
  • Strings use single quotes. Numbers are unquoted.
  • WHERE reduces rows returned; it does not change column selection.
  • Test complex filters incrementally to avoid logic errors.
Common mistake
Writing OR 'Math' without a column comparison makes the expression always true.

screens.title: Comparison operators
screens.narratorSegment: Comparison operators allow you to express simple relationships between values in the WHERE clause. The most common are equals, not-equals, greater-than, less-than, and their or-equals variants. Use equals to match exact values, for example finding students whose Major equals a specific string. Use greater-than and less-than for numeric thresholds, like selecting products with Price greater than 100. Not-equals excludes matches and can be written as either not-equals or the angle-bracket form depending on the database, but both express the same idea. A concrete example: selecting items where StockQuantity is less than 100 helps identify low inventory. A frequent confusion is expecting string comparisons to ignore case; default behavior depends on the database collation and may be case-sensitive, so check your environment. Takeaway: choose the operator that matches your intent, test with sample rows, and remember how strings and numbers are treated differently. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: String vs numeric literals
screens.narratorSegment: One of the most important practical rules when writing WHERE clauses is the difference between string and numeric literals. Strings must be wrapped in single quotes while numbers should be unquoted. If you put quotes around a number, the database will typically perform an implicit conversion or treat it as a string, which can change how comparisons behave and sometimes cause errors. For example, when filtering for Price greater than one hundred, write the numeric 100 without quotes. But when filtering for a Major equal to Computer Science, write the major as a quoted string. A common mistake is to quote numeric thresholds out of habit or to forget quotes on strings. Concrete example: using a quoted year in a numeric PublicationYear comparison could lead to incorrect matches or type coercion. screens.title: Combining conditions with AND, OR, NOT
screens.narratorSegment: Logical operators let you combine multiple conditions in a WHERE clause. AND requires both conditions to be true, OR accepts either condition, and NOT negates a condition. Together they let you express precise sets, for example students who are both Computer Science majors and have a GPA above a threshold. A concrete example: to find Computer Science students with GPA above 3.5 you combine Major equals Computer Science AND GPA greater than 3.5. Another example uses OR to select multiple majors. A common pitfall is forgetting to repeat the column name on each side of OR, which leads to always-true expressions. Also, NOT affects only the condition it precedes, which can be confusing without parentheses. Best practice: build complex conditions in steps and use parentheses to make precedence explicit. Takeaway: AND narrows results, OR widens them, and NOT flips a condition — use parentheses to ensure the logic matches your intention. Combining conditions with AND, OR, NOT means and narrows, or widens, not excludes. use parentheses to control order and avoid accidental matches.. Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › AND / OR / NOT
Examples

SELECT FirstName, LastName, GPA
FROM Students
WHERE Major = 'Computer Science' AND GPA > 3.5;

-- OR example

FROM Students

Notes and pitfalls

  • Test combined conditions on small samples to confirm results.
Pro tip
Build complex filters incrementally: start with one condition, then add AND/OR and re-run the query.

screens.title: Operator precedence and parentheses
screens.narratorSegment: Logical operators have a default order of evaluation: NOT first, then AND, then OR. This order can produce surprising results if you rely on it implicitly. A common example is combining AND and OR without parentheses; the AND binds more tightly and may produce unexpected rows. To avoid ambiguity, use parentheses to group conditions explicitly. Concrete scenario: you want Computer Science students with high GPAs or any Biology majors. Writing the condition with parentheses ensures the intended grouping: either the student is a high-GPA Computer Science major, or the student is a Biology major. Without parentheses you may get a different set of rows because AND would be evaluated before OR. Misconception: parentheses are only optional; in practice they are a readability and correctness tool. Takeaway: always use parentheses for complex logical combinations and read the condition aloud to confirm meaning before running a query that will be used for reporting or decision-making. Operator precedence and parentheses means not > and > or. use parentheses to make intention explicit and avoid accidental matches.. In practical terms, control evaluation order to avoid logic errors. Example with parentheses

FROM Students

Starter templates

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will learn how to speak to relational databases using S Q L. S Q L is a declarative language, which means you tell the database what you want rather than how to get it. You'll learn three fundamentals: how to name the columns you need with SELECT, how to tell the database which table to read from with FROM, and how to narrow the rows returned with WHERE. These three clauses form the backbone of most queries you will write. We'll see concrete examples using a Students table and a Products table, compare selecting every column versus specific columns, and practice common filters using numeric and string comparisons. Along the way I'll point out small mistakes that commonly change results, like forgetting to repeat the column name when using OR, or mixing strings and numbers. By the end you'll be able to write clear read-only queries that retrieve precisely the data needed for reports, UIs, or analysis. Think of S Q L as asking a very literal librarian for the exact pages you need—being precise saves time and avoids errors.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to construct basic read-only S Q L queries against a single table. You will learn to use SELECT to pick the exact columns you need, and to use FROM to identify which table provides that data. You will apply the WHERE clause with comparison operators to filter rows, and you will combine those conditions using logical operators such as AND, OR, and NOT. Each objective is practical: selecting only needed columns reduces data transfer; writing correct WHERE filters prevents returning the wrong set of rows; combining operators with parentheses controls precedence and avoids logic errors. For each skill we include a small mnemonic or visual hint so you remember the pattern. These objectives map directly to common tasks like extracting student names, finding products above a price threshold, or producing lists for reporting. Finally, each objective has a verified competency milestone so you know when you are ready to move on.

These second objectives focus on correct usage and safety. You will distinguish selecting every column with the asterisk from selecting specific columns and understand the performance and privacy tradeoffs. You will learn comparison operators such as equals, not equals, greater than and less than, and see how they behave with strings versus numbers. You will practice logical operators and the correct use of parentheses to control evaluation order. That matters because a misplaced OR can turn a narrow filter into a broad one and return unrelated rows. Each objective includes a short example to rehearse: inspect all columns with the asterisk for debugging, list only first and last names for a roster, filter GPAs above a threshold, and combine department and experience filters safely. These skills help you write queries that are fast, readable, and less likely to leak extra information during debugging or production reports.

S Q L stands for Structured Query Language and it is the standard way to communicate with relational databases. Unlike an imperative language where you specify step-by-step how to compute a result, S Q L is declarative: you describe the result you want and the database figures out the best way to deliver it. That distinction matters because it changes how you think about problems. For example, when you ask for student first and last names, you don't tell the database how to scan files or which index to use. You simply say you want those columns from the Students table and optionally which rows to keep. A common misconception is to treat S Q L like a general-purpose programming language and try to write procedural loops inside queries; instead, keep logic expressed as set-based operations and filters. Concrete example: to list every student's name you declare the columns and the table; you do not loop through rows in application code and build results manually. Takeaway: thinking declaratively leads to simpler queries and lets the database optimize execution. Question to carry forward: what difference does declarative style make when tables contain millions of rows?

The SELECT clause specifies the columns you want to retrieve from a table. At its simplest you can list column names separated by commas, which returns only those fields for every row. Listing columns is useful when you want to limit network transfer or simplify results for a report. A common beginner step is to use SELECT with the Students table to get first and last names. Concrete example: a query that selects FirstName and LastName from Students returns only those two columns for every student. A frequent misconception is to assume columns will be returned in alphabetical order—S Q L returns columns in the order you list them. Also remember that selecting fewer columns is not only cleaner but faster when tables are wide. The code panel shows a small walkthrough starting with selecting all columns for inspection and then narrowing to specific columns. Takeaway: prefer explicit column lists in production, and use the all-columns form only for quick exploration. How might you choose columns differently for a public report versus an internal debug session? SELECT basics means list only the columns you need. this reduces data size and improves clarity and performance.. In practical terms, how to choose which columns to retrieve. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Using the asterisk in SELECT returns every column from the specified table. This is useful for quick exploration, debugging, or when you genuinely need all fields. However, there are important tradeoffs: returning unnecessary columns increases data transfer and can unintentionally expose sensitive fields during development. Conversely, selecting specific columns is explicit, easier to read, and often faster because the database can avoid reading wide fields. Concrete example: selecting all columns from Students might return SocialSecurity or other private attributes you didn't intend to show. A common beginner mistake is leaving SELECT * in code that runs in production, thereby sending extra data to an A P I or UI. Another subtle point is that selecting specific columns preserves column order as you expect; S Q L will present columns in the sequence you list. Takeaway: use the asterisk sparingly and prefer explicit lists for stable, secure queries. Ask yourself: which columns are truly required for this view or report? The FROM clause identifies the table that contains the columns you requested. It is essential because column names mean nothing without the context of a table. If two tables share a column name, the FROM clause plus table-qualified column names resolve ambiguity. A simple example: when you write FROM Students, the database knows to look for columns such as FirstName or GPA on that table. The WHERE clause filters which rows are returned by the query. It appears after FROM and contains one or more conditions built from comparison operators.
